newsitem.title: FRANCE: Price row holds up Internet access on French cable.
newsitem.headline: Price row holds up Internet access on French cable.

text.p: A pricing row is delaying French cable television firms from offering Internet access on their networks, the companies involved say.

The two cable companies complained earlier this month to telecommunications regulator ART (Autorite de Regulation des Telecommunications) that the price asked by France Telecom for a high-speed gateway to cyberspace was too high.
ART is due to rule in July on the complaints from Lyonnaise Cable, part of Lyonnaise des Eaux, and Compagnie Generale de Videocommunication (CGV), part of Generale des Eaux.

France Telecom, which offers its own rival Internet service, owns two-thirds of France's cable networks, and rents two-thirds of the cable it owns to Lyonnaise Cable and CGV which operate cable television services.
Lyonnaise Cable hopes to provide its cable TV subscribers in Paris with Internet access in the autumn, via a cable it rents from France Telecom.
The company already offers Internet access on networks it owns in three French provincial towns, but to date has only 650 Internet users, a spokesman said.
However, it already has a waiting list of 13,000 subscribers seeking Internet access in Paris, he added.
"France Telecom is asking a rental that is too high for the project to be profitable," the Lyonnaise spokesman said.

CGV wants to offer Internet access on cable networks in 15 of the 30 largest French towns, where it rents some two-thirds of the networks from France Telecom, said Stephane Treppoz, TV and multimedia manager at CGV parent Generale des Eaux.
He told Reuters France Telecom was asking far more for the service than "what we calculated would be a fair remuneration".

A France Telecom spokesman said the company was not blocking the development of Internet via cable networks, but needed to charge that much to reflect investments it would have to make to create two-way traffic on the line.
"People are constantly saying we are holding back development. It is not true.... we want to develop Internet by all means available," he said.
He could give no figure for the scale of investment needed to make traffic on a cable channel two-way.

Treppoz said CGV's submission to the regulator offers to finance the necessary investments, which he said would come to "several tens of millions of francs," and to pay France Telecom according to the number of Internet connection plugs it installs.
If it finds the regulator's response satisfactory, it will launch Internet via TV cable across its networks before the end of this year, he said.

French satellite television services are also working on providing Internet access. This plus bringing the Internet to cable TV subscribers will diversify a French multimedia market which was slow to adopt the Net.
Apart from the U.S. service providers, France Telecom's Wanadoo, Lagardere's Club Internet and small independent Infonie are the main home-grown players using telephone lines to access the Net.

The Lyonnaise spokesman said Internet access via TV cables is significantly faster than via telephone lines, because TV cables are the highest capacity lines available. The cyber-surfer can still be reached on the phone, he added.
"It's like a Ferrari compared to a Deux Chevaux," he said.
